title: The practices you kept

segments.voice: Yesterday: the stories you kept. Your line was these stayed. Did you tell your story to someone, and end with where it came from? Day three hundred twenty-seven.

Think of every practice you've tried this year. Watching the breath. Longer out than in. The morning preview and the evening review. Sorting what's in your control. Gratitude. The view from above. Walking, the body scan, a weekly act of service, a screen-free sabbath, the sunset pause. The kettle, the log, the stranger you wished well. That's a lot. If you tried to do all of them every day, you'd need a second life to live in. And here's the honest truth: most of them didn't survive. Real life, with its work and kids and colds and bad weeks, sorted them for you. Today: the practices you kept.
screen: `EVERY PRACTICE YOU TRIED.` → `YOU'D NEED A SECOND LIFE.` → `REAL LIFE SORTED THEM.`

segments.voice: First, survival is information. When a practice keeps happening without much effort, it's telling you something: it fits your life, it hooks onto a cue you already have, and it gives back enough to be worth it. When a practice keeps dying, that's information too. Not a verdict on you. Maybe the timing was wrong, or it was too heroic, or it simply isn't yours. Remember your own evidence. Second, fewer is stronger. A practice done most days for years will shape you more than ten practices tried for a week each. The habit research said about sixty-six days, roughly, for something to become automatic. That's hard to do with ten things at once. It's quite doable with two. Third, the old sorting. Epictetus began his handbook with a single cut, in George Long's translation: "Of things some are in our power, and others are not." The whole Stoic practice starts by sorting. You can use the same knife on your practices: which ones are really in your power to keep, this year, with this life? Keep those. The Buddha's raft story makes a similar point from its own house: a raft is for crossing the river, not for carrying on your head afterward. Some practices did their job and can be set down with thanks. Fourth, dropping isn't losing. The practices you set down stay in you. You know how to do a body scan now. If a hard month comes, you can pick it back up. Keeping two isn't giving up on the others. It's choosing what to carry up the next hill.
screen: `SURVIVAL IS INFORMATION.` · `FEWER IS STRONGER.` · `SOME ARE IN OUR POWER.` · `SET DOWN WITH THANKS.` · then, large: `WHAT SURVIVED.`

segments.voice: Let the year's practices pass through your mind, one by one, like cards. For each, just notice: did this one survive? Don't argue. Then choose two. The two that already happen most, or that you'd miss most. Say them to yourself. Then, silently, thank the rest and set them down. They're not gone; they're on the shelf. The bell holds the time.
The practices you kept. The few that survived real life. Keep two, set the rest down with thanks. Today's word.
Your line: what survived. Write your two practices somewhere you'll see them every day, and do both today, even small. Day three hundred twenty-seven.

howItsDone: People who keep a long-term practice usually settle on a small number of daily practices that fit their lives, and return to others during particular seasons or hard times.
